title: Short Stuff: Salute the Grilled Cheese
summary: Short Stuff episode on the history of the grilled cheese sandwich. Josh and Chuck (with Jerry standing in for Dave) open with tips on fontina cheese and mayonnaise versus butter as the fat. They trace the sandwich from ancient Roman mentions and the French croque monsieur, through sliced bread (Otto Frederick Rohwedder) and Kraft processed cheese (James L. Kraft, 1914 plant in Illinois, sliced cheese in the 1950s), Depression-era open-faced versions, and early recipes such as Sarah Tyson Rorer's (1902), Florence A. Coles's "Seven Hundred Sandwiches," the Boston Cooking School cookbook, and Irma Rombauer's waffle-iron version. The hosts discuss cheese-to-bread ratios, dipping in tomato soup and French onion soup, and close with Kraft's 2007 grilled cheese marketing push, a MySpace video contest winner, and a 2004 online casino's $20,000 purchase of a grilled cheese said to resemble the Virgin Mary.
topics: Stuff You Should Know short stuff

segments.title: Opening banter and fontina tip
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode and the hosts chat about grilled cheese with fontina and mayonnaise instead of butter, plus a brief croque monsieur tangent.

segments.title: Sliced bread and Kraft processed cheese
segments.summary: The hosts credit sliced bread (Otto Frederick Rohwedder) and Kraft's pre-sliced processed cheese, which was popular with the Navy, for helping grilled cheese take off, noting Depression-era open-faced versions.

segments.title: Grilled cheese's rise in the 1950s and 1960s
segments.summary: Grilled cheese became common in America in the 1950s and 1960s, and the hosts note that the modern form dates to that period while earlier recipes were open-faced.

segments.title: Early recipes and the evolution of the grilled cheese
segments.summary: Early recipes from about 1902 onward, including Sarah Tyson Rorer's cheese toast, Florence A. Coles's broiled version, the Boston Cooking School cookbook, and Irma Rombauer's waffle-iron method, lead to the butter-in-a-pan style.

segments.title: Cheese-to-bread ratio and soup dipping
segments.summary: The hosts discuss personal preferences for cheese thickness and bread ratio, and dipping grilled cheese in tomato soup and French onion soup.

segments.title: Grilled cheese trivia: Kraft marketing, MySpace contest, Virgin Mary sandwich
segments.summary: Kraft spent heavily in 2007 to promote grilled cheese, with a MySpace contest won by Chris Gia Maloney. A 2004 online casino bought a grilled cheese said to look like the Virgin Mary for $20,000.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and mention the show's book.
